title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Ten Years of Numbers—Margin Leverage, Debt & Cash Forensics

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, operating profit is sanity, and free cash flow after growth capex is reality.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: A 10-year check of Eli Lilly's audited books (2016–2025) shows one of the sharpest profit swings in big-cap history. From 2016 to 2019, Lilly was a slow-growth drugmaker earning $20.0 billion to $22.3 billion in sales and $2.0 billion to $5.0 billion in operating profit. Starting in 2020, and speeding up in 2023, sales more than tripled from $21,222 million (2016) to $65,179 million (2025). Operating profit grew eightfold from $3,261 million to $26,302 million.

web_blocks.caption: Eli Lilly 10-Year Audited Financial Forensics (FY2016–FY2025, $ Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: Over 10 years, revenue grew 3.07x (13.3% CAGR) while operating income grew 8.07x (26.1% CAGR) as operating margin expanded 2,500 bps from 15.4% to 40.4%. Note: 2017 net loss reflected U.S. tax reform charges; 2019 net income included Elanco divestiture gains.

web_blocks.html: Three key points stand out from the 10-year numbers. First, R&D stayed tight even in rapid growth. Annual R&D rose from $5,244 million (24.7% of sales) in 2016 to $13,337 million in 2025, yet fell to 20.5% of sales as revenue surged. Second, SG&A (MS&A) fell from ~30% of sales in 2016 to 17.0% ($11,094 million) in 2025, showing strong sales scale. Third, 2023–2025 operating profit absorbed $2.9B–$3.8B per year in upfront Acquired IPR&D costs. Core operating margin excluding those deal charges is even higher than 40.4%.

Cash conversion also needs a close look. In FY2025, Operating Cash Flow ($16,813 million) trailed GAAP Net Income ($20,640 million) by $3,827 million (81.5% conversion), much like 2023–2024. That gap is not an earnings red flag. It reflects higher receivables and API stock needed to support +45% sales growth, plus tax timing. Even after $7,841 million in PPE capex (up 4.2x from 2021), Free Cash Flow more than doubled in FY2025 to $8,972 million.

On the balance sheet, Lilly used investment-grade debt to fund its >$50 billion plant plan without issuing stock. Total debt grew from $16.24 billion at end-2022 to $25.23 billion (2023), $33.64 billion (2024), and $42.50 billion at end-2025 ($40.87 billion long-term), with $895 million in FY2025 gross interest. Against $26,302 million in FY2025 operating profit and ~$28.3 billion in EBITDA ($26,302M EBIT + $1,997M D&A), gross debt is a safe ~1.5x EBITDA and interest coverage tops 29x. Meanwhile, diluted shares fell from 911.7 million (2021) to 899.3 million (2025) via $4,105 million in FY2025 buybacks. Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) hit 31.6%, more than triple an 8.5%–9.0% cost of capital.

Capital allocation from 2021 to 2025 follows a clear 'reinvest first, return excess' rule. In FY2025, Lilly put $13,337 million into R&D, $7,841 million into PPE capex, and ~$3,000 million into acquired IPR&D deals—nearly $24.2 billion in total growth spend. It still returned cash via $4,105 million in buybacks and a rising dividend (15.2% 3-year/5-year growth, 26.1% payout ratio).

Asset efficiency and taxes round out the picture. Lilly's effective tax rate normalized to 19.79% in FY2025 ($5,091 million on $25,731 million pretax profit) as U.S. and European profit mix rose. Its $40,868 million in long-term debt ($42,500 million total) carries fixed coupons and spread-out due dates. Liquidity stays healthy (1.39x current ratio, 1.00x quick ratio), and 1.23x debt-to-equity is backed by 86.1% ROE and 31.6% ROIC.

Comparing 2016–2019 against 2023–2025 also shows the strength of Lilly's dividend and capital returns. Dividends per share grew at a ~15.2% 3-year and 5-year CAGR while using just 26.1% of profit. That leaves nearly three-quarters of earnings to compound at >30% ROIC. Even if capex stays at 10%–12% of sales through 2027, operating cash flow easily funds plants, R&D, and debt service.

Taken together, the 10-year record proves Lilly is not riding a brief price spike. Its margin gains rest on 83% gross-margin unit economics, tight R&D and SG&A control, and smart spending on plants and late-stage drugs.

Q3 2026 10-Q forensics update three balance-sheet and cash-flow items beyond FY2025. First, following the May 20, 2026 $9.0 billion Senior Notes offering ($8,941 million net proceeds), total debt rose from $42,503 million at end-2025 to $49,503 million at September 30, 2026 ($2,517 million short-term plus $46,986 million long-term), while cash stood at $4,885 million. Second, accrued sales rebates and discounts surged 39% in nine months from $17,382 million to $24,170 million, and maximum contingent consideration from 2026 acquisitions reached $5,292 million ($3,750 million Kelonia, $1,542 million Centessa). Third, 9M 2026 Operating Cash Flow more than doubled YoY to $27,420 million against $8,437 million in PPE CapEx ($18,983 million 9M Free Cash Flow), even as $7,541 million in nondeductible Acquired IPR&D ($4,181 million in Q3 alone) lifted the Q3 2026 effective tax rate to 23.3%.

book_paragraphs: If you and I want to separate a genuine compounder from a promotional story, we always end our business audit in the 10-year financial statements. Stories can be spun in investor presentations; ten years of audited cash flows, margins, and balance-sheet debt cannot.

Look at Eli Lilly's trajectory from 2016 through 2025. For the first four years of that decade, Lilly looked like a classic mature pharma company: $20 billion to $22 billion in revenue, 15% to 22% operating margins, and modest free cash flow. Then the incretin flywheel caught fire. Between 2022 and 2025 alone, revenue more than doubled from $28.5 billion to $65.2 billion, and operating income nearly quadrupled from $7.1 billion to $26.3 billion.

Updating our forensic ledger through the September 30, 2026 Form 10-Q reveals both surging cash generation and heavier balance-sheet commitments. Nine-month Operating Cash Flow jumped to $27,420 million (versus $13,588 million in 9M 2025), funding $8,437 million in PPE CapEx and leaving $18,983 million in 9M Free Cash Flow. At the same time, total debt expanded to $49,503 million after May 2026's $9.0 billion bond issuance, accrued sales rebates and discounts climbed 39% to $24,170 million, and $7,541 million of nondeductible 9M Acquired IPR&D pushed the Q3 2026 effective tax rate up to 23.3%.

book_subsections.title: The Margin Bridge & Operating Leverage
paragraphs: How does a 150-year-old manufacturer expand operating margins by 2,500 basis points—from 15.4% in 2016 to 40.4% in 2025? Two forces worked together. First, gross margin climbed into the low-80s (83.04% in FY2025) as high-value patented incretins and oncology therapies dominated the mix. Second, Lilly held the line on overhead: while internal R&D more than doubled in dollar terms from $5.24 billion to $13.34 billion, R&D as a percentage of sales actually fell from 24.7% to 20.5%. Marketing, selling, and administrative costs compressed even faster, down to 17.0% of sales.

Even more impressive, that 40.4% GAAP operating margin in FY2025 was achieved after expensing $2,910 million in Acquired IPR&D directly through the income statement. Under modern accounting rules, upfront payments for early-stage biotech collaborations are expensed immediately rather than capitalized, which understates Lilly's true underlying core operating profitability by more than four percentage points.

book_subsections.title: Cash Conversion, Debt & Capital Efficiency
paragraphs: A sharp forensic analyst always asks: why did FY2025 Operating Cash Flow ($16.81 billion) lag Net Income ($20.64 billion) by $3.83 billion? In a slower-growing business, a persistent gap between CFO and Net Income can signal aggressive revenue recognition. At Lilly, the explanation is straightforward working-capital physics: when revenue jumps $20 billion in a single year (+44.7%), accounts receivable and peptide/API inventories naturally absorb billions of dollars of cash. Even after that working-capital build and $7.84 billion in PPE capital expenditures, Lilly generated $8.97 billion in Free Cash Flow.

To finance its $50 billion+ U.S. factory buildout without issuing equity, management tapped the bond market, taking total debt from $16.24 billion in 2022 to $42.50 billion in 2025. On paper, a $26 billion debt increase looks aggressive—until you compare it to Lilly's earnings power. At roughly 1.5x EBITDA with 29x EBIT interest coverage and a 31.6% Return on Invested Capital, that debt is comfortably serviced and productively deployed, while diluted shares actually shrank from 911.7 million in 2021 to 899.3 million in 2025.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Working-Capital & Capex Normalization Ahead
callouts.text: Notice what happens to Lilly's Free Cash Flow when revenue growth naturally moderates from 45% toward 15%–20% and the $50 billion factory buildout passes peak construction: working-capital drag eases, capex intensity steps down from 12% of sales toward maintenance levels, and FCF conversion should snap back toward 90%–100% of Net Income.

book_subsections.title: Capital Allocation Hierarchy: $24 Billion Reinvested Before a Dollar of Buybacks
paragraphs: When you and I study capital allocation, we look at the order in which management writes checks. In FY2025, Lilly wrote its first check to the lab ($13.34 billion in internal R&D), its second check to the factory floor ($7.84 billion in PPE capex), and its third check to external biotech partners ($3.0 billion in cash IPR&D). Only after funding $24.2 billion of high-return organic and bolt-on growth did management allocate $4.11 billion to share buybacks and maintain its 15%-annual-growth dividend at a conservative 26% payout ratio.

That hierarchy is textbook compounding. When a business earns 31.6% on invested capital, the worst thing management can do is starve its own factories and labs to engineer short-term EPS via leveraged buybacks. Lilly used investment-grade debt prudently—keeping leverage around 1.5x EBITDA—so it never had to choose between building capacity and rewarding patient shareholders.

book_subsections.title: What to Verify in 2026–2027 Filings
paragraphs: As we close Pass 1 and prepare for valuation and market-pricing analysis in Pass 2, keep three accounting items on your forensic watchlist: first, whether Q4 2026 and FY2027 working-capital absorption eases as revenue growth moderates from 45% toward 20%–30%; second, whether Acquired IPR&D charges remain around $3 billion–$4 billion annually or spike higher; and third, how rapidly depreciation climbs as the $50 billion U.S. manufacturing wave transitions from construction-in-progress onto the income statement.

book_subsections.title: The Forensic Verdict Before Valuation
paragraphs: Take a step back and look at the entire ten-year financial arc we just audited. Between 2016 and 2025, Eli Lilly tripled its revenue from $21.2 billion to $65.2 billion, expanded its operating margin by 2,500 basis points to 40.4%, grew net income more than sevenfold to $20.6 billion, and lifted its Return on Invested Capital to 31.6%. It did all of that while doubling annual R&D investment to $13.3 billion and funding $7.84 billion in annual factory capex—without issuing a single net share of dilutive equity.

Are there real financial risks to watch? Absolutely. Total debt stands at $42.5 billion, working capital absorbed nearly $3.8 billion of cash flow in 2025, and depreciation will climb as new plants come online. Yet against $26.3 billion of operating income and $8.97 billion of free cash flow, the balance sheet is built on solid rock. Our price-blind business verdict is clear: Eli Lilly passes every quality gate as a premier structural compounder.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Balance Sheet Behind the $50 Billion Buildout
paragraphs: A skeptical reader looking at Lilly's balance sheet sees $42.5 billion of gross debt and a 1.23 debt-to-equity ratio—higher leverage than Eli Lilly carried a decade ago. Context matters here. With trailing operating income above $36 billion and EBITDA exceeding $46 billion, net leverage sits comfortably around 1.5x EBITDA, well within investment-grade territory.

More importantly, that capital was not borrowed to fund share buybacks or overpriced acquisitions. It built hard, revenue-producing U.S. manufacturing plants that earn a 31.61% return on invested capital. As peak construction spending tapers between 2027 and 2029, free cash flow conversion—currently depressed to 43.5% of net income by $7.84 billion of FY2025 PPE capex—should normalize toward 75%–85%.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Price-Blind Business Verdict
book_callouts.text: Standing back from the entire six-chapter business audit—without looking at a single stock price or valuation multiple—Eli Lilly earns an unambiguous COMPOUNDER_PASS. It combines 83% gross margins, 40% operating margins, 31.6% ROIC, a multi-modality metabolic moat, and disciplined capital allocation. Our next job in Pass 2 will be to test what price is already baked into the market.
